name: Mecasermin rinfabate
lead: Mecasermin rinfabate (brand name Iplex, also called rhIGF-I/rhIGFBP-3) is a complex of recombinant human insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) bound to recombinant IGF binding protein 3, given by daily subcutaneous injection. It was developed by Insmed to prolong the half-life of IGF-1 and potentially reduce side effects such as hypoglycemia [3][11].

Its original target was growth failure in children with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or growth hormone insensitivity [4][11]. According to Wikipedia, the product was withdrawn from the market for short-stature indications following a patent settlement, and research moved to other conditions [11].

Clinical work in the sources covers myotonic dystrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, retinopathy of prematurity and other conditions [12][13][14]. It is discussed in this wiki because of interest in height and bone growth; the sources contain no data on use for height in people with normal IGF-1 and no looksmaxxing forum discussion.

For height, the relevant chain runs through growth hormone and IGF-1: growth hormone acts at the growth plate partly by stimulating IGF-1, so a drug that supplies IGF-1 was developed for children whose short stature comes from IGF-1 deficiency rather than from lack of growth hormone [4]. Reviews report that both mecasermin and mecasermin rinfabate raise growth velocity in children with severe primary IGF deficiency [5][2].

paras: Severe primary IGF-1 deficiency includes growth hormone insensitivity syndrome (Laron syndrome), in which the body does not respond to growth hormone and so makes too little IGF-1 [7][2]. The FDA-approved indication described in reviews also covered children with a growth hormone gene deletion who developed neutralizing antibodies to growth hormone [5]. In these groups, treatment with IGF-1, alone or bound to its binding protein, increased growth velocity [5][2].

The product was developed for those children, not for people whose growth is within the normal range. Interest in it among height-focused readers comes from its relationship to the growth hormone and IGF-1 axis, but the published literature describes patient populations only.

Insmed Corporation developed the complex under the trade name Iplex, and an earlier development name was SomatoKine [11][7]. A Drugs in R&D profile described the most advanced indication as severe growth disorders from growth hormone insensitivity syndrome [7]. Wikipedia records that, after a patent settlement, Iplex was being withdrawn from the market for short-stature indications, and that the company's work turned to other conditions [11].

One of those conditions was amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). According to Wikipedia, in January 2007 Insmed said the Italian Ministry of Health had asked it to supply Iplex for Italian ALS patients, and on 11 March 2009 the FDA announced it would be made available to Americans with ALS within a clinical trial [11]. Results of a two-year, placebo-controlled trial in 330 patients at 20 US centers, led by Eric Sorenson of the Mayo Clinic, were published in Neurology in November 2008; the trial reported no difference from placebo in muscle strength, tracheostomy need or survival [11].

Growth hormone acts at the growth plate directly and through IGF-1, and a large share of the hormone circulates bound to binding proteins [4]. Binding IGF-1 to IGFBP-3 was intended to prolong its circulation and reduce adverse effects relative to IGF-1 alone (mecasermin) [3]. Drug reviews describe its pharmacokinetics, safety profile and efficacy [3][5][6].

In the body IGF-1 circulates mostly bound to IGFBP-3, which governs delivery to tissues and releases IGF-1 when proteases clip the binding protein [7]. Reviews note that unbound recombinant IGF-1 had a shorter half-life in patients with growth hormone insensitivity, who have low IGFBP-3, and was associated with hypoglycemia; the complex was designed to prolong half-life and counter that effect [5][2]. One review found no studies comparing mecasermin with mecasermin rinfabate head to head, though both had been shown effective [2]. Another concluded that the biological effects and side-effect profile of the complex were largely similar to IGF-1 alone, with little published pharmacokinetic data in humans [3].

The initial indication was growth failure from severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, including children with growth hormone gene deletion who developed neutralizing antibodies [4][11]. Wikipedia reports a phase II study in myotonic muscular dystrophy that found increased muscle weight but no improvement in grip strength or walking tests, with lab changes including higher testosterone and LDL and lower triglycerides and HDL [11]. Registered studies include phase 1/2 trials in myotonic dystrophy (NCT00233519) [12] and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (NCT01207908) [13], and phase 2 trials of IGF-1/IGFBP-3 for prevention of complications of prematurity such as retinopathy of prematurity (NCT01096784, NCT03253263) [14][15].
Wikipedia states that the complex was reported to have fewer side effects, such as hypoglycemia, than mecasermin alone [11]. A fuller safety profile is described in drug reviews [3][6].

Human studies have examined growth disorders, myotonic dystrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and prematurity-related conditions [3][11][12][13][14][15]. No studies of mecasermin rinfabate for height gain or bone length in people with normal growth were found.

Outside growth disorders, reviews describe studies of the complex in diabetes, severe insulin resistance, osteopenia, burns and growth hormone insensitivity, with outcomes similar to IGF-1 alone [3]. Registered trials include a phase 1/2 study in 17 people with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (NCT00233519, started 2005), a phase 1/2 study in 44 people with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (NCT01207908, started 2010), a phase 2 retinopathy of prematurity study of 121 infants (NCT01096784, started 2010) with a long-term follow-up of 76 children (NCT02386839), and a phase 2 study of the complex as OHB-607 in 295 extremely premature infants (NCT03253263, started 2019) [12][13][14][15][16]. A 2026 Cochrane review addresses IGF-1 for preventing or treating retinopathy of prematurity [17].

timeline.event: Insmed's development program for rhIGF-I/rhIGFBP-3 in growth hormone insensitivity is profiled; the myotonic dystrophy trial starts in November [7][12].
Two-year ALS trial results are published in Neurology, reporting no difference from placebo [11].
FDA announces Iplex will be available to US ALS patients within a clinical trial [11].
A phase 2 trial of the complex (OHB-607) begins in extremely premature infants [15].

card.summary: An IGF-1/IGFBP-3 injectable built for rare growth failure; no data supports height gain in people with normal growth.
card.note: Withdrawn for short-stature indications; no data for normal-height use.

quick.overview:
Mecasermin rinfabate (Iplex) pairs recombinant IGF-1 with its binding protein and is injected under the skin. Insmed developed it for children with severe IGF-1 deficiency.

It was withdrawn for short-stature indications after a patent settlement, and trials moved to muscular dystrophy and prematurity conditions. No studies address height in people with normal growth.
quick.mechanism: Binding IGF-1 to IGFBP-3 was designed to extend how long IGF-1 stays in circulation and to reduce side effects such as low blood sugar.
quick.risks: Reported effects in trials included lab changes such as higher testosterone and LDL in myotonic dystrophy patients. It is a prescription biologic, and published safety data come from patient populations.
